overview: The Sena dynasty made Bengal a major regional kingdom during the late eleventh and twelfth centuries. Its rulers supported Sanskrit learning, temples and land grants. The imported 1000 to 1200 interval starts too early and ends before Sena rule disappeared.

periods.title: Before consolidated Sena rule
periods.summary: The map begins before the securely documented late-eleventh-century rise of the dynasty.

periods.title: Vijayasena expands power
periods.summary: Vijayasena displaced Pala and Varman power across much of Bengal.

periods.title: Ballala and Lakshmana
periods.summary: Vallalasena and Lakshmanasena continued the dynasty; its political history extends beyond this map window.

sections.title: Reading the kingdom and its records

items.text: The shaded territory is misplaced east of the Sena heartland: it runs roughly from 91 to 95 degrees east, across areas toward northeastern India and Myanmar. It should not be used as a reliable Sena boundary. The dynasty’s documented centers and grants belong to Bengal.

The Deopara inscription praises Vijayasena’s campaigns and describes a fleet on the Ganga. It also boasts of victories on an enormous scale. This is royal praise poetry: evidence of what the court wanted remembered, with its claims read more carefully than a modern campaign map.

A copper land-grant document could carry its own religious badge. One surviving Sena plate has a ten-armed Shiva seal attached above its Sanskrit text. The grant rewarded Udayakaradeva Sharman for a ritual performed for Queen Vilasa Devi during a lunar eclipse.

sections.title: Homes, fields and the working landscape

items.text: The Naihati grant describes a village with homesteads, cultivated fields and fallow ground. Its boundaries follow the Singatia River, embankments and cattle paths. A path made by everyday animal traffic could matter enough to be recorded in a royal legal document.

The same charter values annual production at 500 puranas in cowries, the small shells used as units of value. It also specifies fiscal rights and exemptions. This was a transfer of income and authority affecting a working village, not merely a ceremonial present with no practical consequences.

The Tarpandighi grant gives an especially watery set of directions: Nicadahara’s pond to the south, Nandiharipa’s reservoir to the west and Mollana’s canal to the north. Water shaped how people described their neighborhood and where one property stopped and another began.

That charter includes areca-nut and coconut trees, woodland, bushes, watering places, grassland and pasture. The landscape was a patchwork of useful resources. A grant was not just a neat rectangle of grain fields; trees, animals and access to water belonged in the accounting too.

Queen Vilasadevi appears as an active donor in the Naihati plate. Her son Vallalasena recorded land she had assigned for a religious gift at a solar eclipse. The document links a mother’s decision, a son’s royal authority and a scholar’s reward.

The Tarpandighi recipient, Isvaradevasarman, is described through his family lineage and his observance of the Kauthuma branch of the Samaveda. Land supported a learned religious specialist. This is concrete evidence of elite scholarship and patronage, rather than a count of schools open to all children.

A neighboring property in that grant belonged to a Buddhist establishment, while the royal donation honored Narayana, a form of Vishnu. The charter places different religious institutions in the same local landscape. It gives a more specific picture than imagining every village following one identical practice.

The Deopara text names both the poet Umapatidhara and the engraver Ranaka Shulapani. It praises Shulapani among Varendra’s artisans and records his father, grandfather and great-grandfather. Behind a king’s polished message were identifiable people skilled in language and stone carving.

Vijayasena’s Deopara eulogy describes the Pradyumneshvara temple and a lake excavated before it. Temples and waterworks were part of the image of a generous ruler. The poem imagines the building reaching fantastically high: impressive praise, not a measurement an engineer should put on a blueprint.

A twelfth-century Bengal sculpture of Durga is only 13.5 centimeters tall, yet the artist fitted sixteen arms and their weapons around the goddess battling a buffalo demon. This small argillite carving shows how much movement a skilled sculptor could pack into a very small space.

A separate stone sculpture, catalogued to the Sena dynasty, represents Jupiter as the figure Brhaspati. At about 56 centimeters tall, it makes a planet into a person who could be encountered in religious art. It is evidence of planetary imagery, not a picture made through a telescope.

At Ballal Dhipi in Bamanpukur, excavations from 1982 to 1988 exposed a large brick complex and objects dated broadly to the tenth through twelfth centuries. The ASI identifies a temple complex and notes copper ritual objects and possibly Buddhist stucco heads. The familiar royal name does not date every layer.

Rainwater needed somewhere to go. A published study of the multiphase Ballal Dhipi site describes plastered channels and a stone outlet shaped like a crocodile’s face. It is a memorable piece of water management, although its precise building phase cannot simply be assigned to King Ballala Sena.

Jayadeva, associated with Lakshmanasena’s court, composed the Gitagovinda about Radha and Krishna. Its twenty-four songs specify musical modes, or ragas, and are linked by narrative passages. Literature could be sung and performed, rather than remaining silent words on a page.

Just after the map’s endpoint, Shridharadasa compiled the Saduktikarnamrita in 1205. It preserves verses by Sena court poets alongside older works, with themes ranging from devotion to familiar landscapes and everyday emotions. An anthology saved many voices that one royal inscription could never contain.

Sanskrit: namaḥ śivāya, “salutation to Shiva.” These words open Vijayasena’s twelfth-century Deopara stone inscription after Om. The original script is Gaudi; this is the scholarly Roman transliteration, not modern Bengali lettering presented as a photograph of the stone.

ending.text: Bakhtiyar Khalji’s attack around 1204 broke Sena power in western Bengal, but Lakshmanasena and his successors retained territory farther east. Later grants document continuing rule there. The dynasty’s contraction unfolded after this map ends; its people, villages, worship and literature continued through changing rulers.
